posts.quote: WE DIDN'T HAVE PLAYDATES. WE HAD "BE HOME BEFORE THE STREETLIGHTS COME ON."
posts.caption: You could be gone from breakfast till supper and nobody called a soul. There was one rule, and it hung over the whole neighborhood like the sky. When that first streetlight buzzed on at the end of the block, every bike on the street turned around at once. You'd hear screen doors slapping shut from three houses down. Nobody owned a watch, but nobody was ever late, either. That light was the most reliable clock in America, and every mother in town had it set to the same time.
posts.first:
Our streetlight was right in front of the Hendersons' house, and it always took a minute to warm up. My brother and I used to argue about whether the flicker counted or whether we had until it went full bright. Mom never once agreed with our interpretation.

posts.quote: FULL SERVICE MEANT SOMEBODY ELSE PUMPED THE GAS, CHECKED THE OIL, AND WASHED THE WINDSHIELD.
posts.caption: You'd pull in, roll over that rubber hose, and a bell would ding somewhere inside the garage. Before your tires stopped rolling, a fellow in a cap was already at your window asking, "Fill 'er up?" He'd check your oil and show you the dipstick like a doctor showing you an X-ray. Then he'd wash the windshield, front and back, and check the air in your tires without being asked. You paid him in cash and he made change out of a coin changer on his belt. Nobody tipped him and nobody expected it. He just figured that's what the job was.
posts.first:
My first real job was at a station on Route 9 the summer I turned sixteen. The owner told me the windshield was the most important part, because it's the last thing the customer looks through when they drive away. I still can't pass a dirty windshield without wanting to fix it.

posts.quote: MY MOTHER HAD A LOOK THAT COULD STOP A FREIGHT TRAIN AT 40 YARDS.
posts.caption: She never had to raise her voice. She didn't have to say a single word. You'd be reaching for something you had no business reaching for, and the back of your neck would just go cold. You'd turn around, and there she was in the doorway with one eyebrow slightly up. That was it. That was the whole sentence. Grown men who worked at the plant with my father were scared of that look, and they'd only seen it once.
posts.first:
I tested the look exactly one time, at my cousin's wedding when I was nine. I made it about two steps toward the cake table before I felt it from across the hall. I sat back down and folded my hands like a choirboy for the rest of the night.

posts.quote: If you heard your full name from the back door, middle name included, you came running. No questions asked.
posts.first:
Mine was "Robert Allen," and when both names came out together, it meant somebody had found the broken flower pot. I don't think I've ever run faster in my life, before or since.

posts.quote: HOME EC AND WOOD SHOP / WE LEARNED TO SEW A HEM AND BUILD A BIRDHOUSE BEFORE WE LEARNED TO DRIVE.
posts.caption: Third period was Home Ec, and the room always smelled like warm sewing machine oil and somebody's burnt cinnamon toast. Down the hall, you could hear the band saw whining in Wood Shop. They taught us to thread a bobbin, balance a checkbook, and plane a board straight without taking a finger off. Nobody called them life skills back then. They were just classes, same as algebra. Half the birdhouses we made were crooked, and every one of them hung in somebody's backyard for twenty years.
posts.first:
I made an apron in Home Ec that my mother wore every Thanksgiving until 1994. The pocket was sewn on slightly crooked, and she said that was her favorite part. When she passed, my sister found it folded in the kitchen drawer.

posts.quote: A NEW PATTERN, A YARD OF GINGHAM, AND A SPOOL OF RICKRACK. SUNDAY WAS GOING TO BE BEAUTIFUL.
posts.caption: The fabric store was the quietest happy place in town. You'd walk in and run your hand along those bolts like you were reading a book. The pattern drawer was a whole afternoon's work, flipping through envelopes until the right dress jumped out at you. The lady at the counter would measure your yard against the brass ruler nailed to the wood, snip it, and tear the rest with one clean pull. Then came the rickrack, the buttons, and a spool of thread matched by holding it up to the window light. By Saturday night the kitchen table was covered in pins. By Sunday morning, you had something nobody else in church was wearing.
posts.first:
My grandmother could look at a dress in a store window and sew it from memory without a pattern. I used to sit under her sewing table and collect the pins she dropped in a little magnet dish. I still have that dish.

posts.quote: THE WAY-BACK OF THE STATION WAGON WAS THE BEST SEAT IN AMERICA.
posts.caption: Mom and Dad got the front. The baby got the middle. But if you were lucky, you got the way-back. Facing backward, waving at every truck driver until one of them blew his horn. You could stretch out on a blanket, play cards, and pretend you were riding a train across the country. When Dad hit the brakes, everything back there slid forward, including you. Nobody ever counted that as a problem. Two hundred miles to Grandma's, and it felt like the best ride at the county fair.
posts.first:
Our wagon was a pale green with fake wood on the sides, and my dad loved it more than he let on. My sister and I worked out a system where we traded the way-back every hundred miles. She cheated by falling asleep so I couldn't move her.

posts.quote: Saturday morning: up before the sun, cereal in a big bowl, cartoons until Mom ran the vacuum right in front of the TV.
posts.first:
We had one TV and three kids, so whoever got up first held the dial. I set no alarm in my life the way I set my own internal clock on Saturdays. I was up at 5:58 every week, sitting cross-legged on the rug, waiting for the test pattern to go away.

posts.quote: BETTER TO BE TEN MINUTES EARLY THAN ONE MINUTE LATE.
posts.caption: In our house, the car started at 9:40 for 10 o'clock church, and it was eight minutes away. My father would be standing by the door with his keys at 9:35, saying nothing. He didn't have to. The whole family moved around him like he was a lighthouse. If you showed up at the same time as everybody else, as far as he was concerned, you were late. He'd say, "Early is respect." We rolled our eyes at it for years. Funny how every one of us ended up the first car in the parking lot.
posts.first:
My dad drove for a dairy for thirty-one years and was never once late for a route. When he retired, they gave him a gold watch, and he laughed because he didn't need it. He'd been running on his own clock his whole life.

posts.character: Humor about today vs. then (the family phone)
posts.quote: ONE PHONE. ONE CORD. SEVEN PEOPLE. / AND EVERYBODY HEARD EVERY WORD.
posts.caption: The phone hung on the kitchen wall, and that's where it stayed. If you wanted privacy, you stretched that curly cord as far down the hallway as it would go and closed the closet door on it. Your little brother was always listening on the extension. Dad was always "just reading the paper" in the next room. When the call ran too long, somebody would start picking up the receiver and setting it down again. We learned to say a whole lot in very few words. Some of the best talks of my life happened sitting on that hallway floor.
posts.first:
Our phone cord got stretched so many times it reached all the way to the basement stairs. My father finally bought a 25-foot replacement and said it was a gift for the whole family. Really, he just wanted the hallway back.
